en: Exposition of the Designation of Human Types 1.
The Designation of Single Human Types
And what kind of person is one liberated by occasion?

Here, a certain person dwells having from time to time, on various occasions, personally experienced the eight liberations; and for him, having seen with wisdom, some of the taints are completely destroyed.
This person is called "one liberated by occasion."
And what kind of person is one liberated at all times (asamayavimutta)?
Here, a certain person does not dwell having from time to time, at every occasion, personally realized the eight liberations; yet, having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
This person is called "one liberated at all times."
All noble persons (ariyapuggala) are liberated at all times in the noble liberations (vimokkha).
And what kind of person is one of a fickle nature (kuppadhamma)?
Here, a certain person is an attainer of meditative attainments (samāpatti) associated with the form realm or associated with the formless realm.
Yet he does not obtain them at will, nor without difficulty, nor without trouble;
nor does he enter into and emerge from them wherever, whenever, or for as long as he wishes.
However, it is possible that through negligence those attainments might fail him.
This person is called one whose nature is subject to disturbance.
And what kind of person is one whose nature is not subject to disturbance?
Here, a certain person is an attainer of meditative attainments (samāpatti) associated with the form realm or associated with the formless realm.
Moreover, he is one who attains them at will, without difficulty, and without trouble;
wherever, whatever, and for as long as he desires, he enters into and emerges from those attainments.
It is impossible, it cannot happen, that those attainments should fail him on account of negligence.
This person is called one "of unshakable nature.
All noble persons (ariyapuggala) are of unshakable nature regarding the noble liberation (vimokkha).
And what kind of person is one "subject to decline"?
Here, a certain person is one who attains meditative absorptions (samāpatti) associated with the form realm or the formless realm.
Yet he does not attain them at will, nor without difficulty, nor without trouble;
he cannot enter or emerge from them whenever, wherever, or for as long as he wishes.
It is indeed possible that such a person, through negligence, might fall away from those attainments;
this person is called "one subject to decline.
And what kind of person is one not subject to decline?
Here, a certain person is an attainer of meditative attainments (samāpatti) accompanied by form or unaccompanied by form.
Moreover, he is one who attains them at will, without difficulty, and without trouble;
wherever, whenever, and for as long as he wishes, he both enters into and emerges from them.
It is impossible, it cannot happen, that such a person, having fallen into negligence, would fall away from those attainments;
this person is called "one whose nature is not subject to falling away.
Indeed, all noble persons (ariyapuggala) are of a nature not subject to falling away from the noble liberation (ariyo vimokkho).
And what kind of person is capable through volition?
Here, a certain person is one who attains meditative absorptions (samāpatti) associated with the form realm or the formless realm.
Yet he does not attain them at will, nor without difficulty, nor without trouble.
He does not enter into or emerge from the attainments wherever, whenever, or for as long as he wishes.
If he maintains his intention, he does not fall away from those attainments;
if he does not maintain his intention, he falls away from those attainments.
This person is called one "capable of volition.
And what kind of person is "capable of preservation"?
Here, a certain person is an attainer of meditative attainments (samāpatti) associated with the form realm or associated with the formless realm.
Yet he does not obtain them at will, nor without difficulty, nor without trouble;
nor does he enter into and emerge from them wherever, whenever, or for as long as he wishes.
But if he guards them, he does not fall away from those attainments.
If he does not guard them, he falls away from those attainments;
such a person is called "one capable of guarding. And what is a worldling (puthujjana)?
The person for whom the three fetters are not abandoned,
and who has not yet entered upon the practice for the abandoning of those states—
this is called a "worldling" (puthujjana).
And what kind of person is one of the lineage (gotrabhū)?
One who possesses those states immediately after which there is the descent into the noble state (ariyadhamma)—
this is called a person of the lineage.
And what kind of person is one restrained by fear?
The seven types of trainees are restrained by fear, as are those worldlings who possess virtuous conduct.
An arahant is one who is not restrained by fear.
And what kind of person is incapable of progress?
Those persons who are possessed of the obstruction of karma, possessed of the obstruction of defilements, and possessed of the obstruction of maturation;
who are faithless, lacking desire for the good, and devoid of wisdom; who are dull-witted and incapable of entering upon the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states.
These are called persons "incapable of progress.
And what kind of person is capable of progress?
Those persons who are not possessed of an obstruction consisting of karma, not possessed of an obstruction consisting of defilements, and not possessed of an obstruction consisting of karmic result.
Endowed with faith, zealous, wise, and not dull-witted, they are capable of entering into the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states—
these persons are called "capable of arrival.
And what kind of person is one who is fixed?
There are five persons who are fixed in their destiny (ānantarika), those who are fixed in wrong view, and the eight noble persons (ariyapuggala) who are fixed in their destiny.
All remaining persons are unfixed.
And what kind of person is one who is practicing (paṭipannaka)?
There are four types of persons who possess the path and are practicing, and four types of persons who possess the fruit and are established in the fruit.
And what kind of person is one with an even head?
It is the person for whom the exhaustion of the taints and the exhaustion of life occur simultaneously, neither before nor after.
This person is called one who is "equal in head.
And what is the person who is a "world-endurer"?

Suppose this person is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, and it is the time for the world-age to end; yet the world-age does not end until this person has realized the fruit of stream-entry. This is the person who is a world-endurer.
This person is called one who "reckons the aeon" (*ṭhitakappī*).
All persons possessing the path are reckoners of the aeon.
And what kind of person is noble (*ariya*)?
The eight noble persons are noble.
The remaining persons are non-noble.
And what kind of person is one in training (sekha)?
The four individuals who possess the paths and the three individuals who possess the fruits are "trainees" (sekha).
The arahant is "beyond training" (asekha).
All remaining individuals are "neither trainee nor beyond training" (nevasekkhanāsekkha).
And what kind of person is one possessed of the three true knowledges?
A person endowed with the three true knowledges is "one possessed of the three true knowledges.
And what kind of person is one possessed of the six direct knowledges?
A person endowed with the six direct knowledges is “one possessing the six direct knowledges.
And what kind of person is a perfectly enlightened Buddha?
Here, a certain person, regarding things unheard before, personally awakens to the truths.
And therein he attains omniscience and mastery over the powers—
this person is called a "Perfectly Enlightened One" (Sammāsambuddha).
And what kind of person is a "Privately Enlightened One" (Paccekasambuddha)?
Here, a certain person awakens by himself to the truths regarding teachings never heard before;
yet he does not attain omniscience therein, nor mastery over the powers.
This person is called a "paccekasambuddha" (a solitary enlightened one).
And what kind of person is one liberated in both ways?
Here, a certain person dwells having personally realized the eight liberations with the body;
and having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
This person is called one "liberated in both ways.
And what kind of person is one liberated by wisdom?
Here, a certain person does not dwell having personally realized the eight liberations with the body; [yet]...
Having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
This person is called one "liberated by wisdom.
And what kind of person is a "body-witness"?
Here, a certain person dwells having personally experienced the eight liberations with the body;
and having seen with wisdom, some of his taints are completely destroyed.
This person is called a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhī).
And what kind of person is one who has attained through vision?
Here, a certain person understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering"; he understands as it really is:
"This is the cessation of suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering."
He understands as it really is: “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
The teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata have been clearly seen and fully mastered by him through wisdom.
Having seen with wisdom, some of his taints are completely destroyed.
This person is called one who has attained through vision (*diṭṭhippatto*).
And what is the person liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutto*)?
Here, a certain person understands as it really is: "This is suffering," and "This is the origin of suffering."
He understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
And the teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata have been clearly seen and fully mastered by him through wisdom.
Having seen with wisdom, some of his taints are completely destroyed, yet not as in the case of one who has attained through vision;
such a person is called "one liberated by faith.
And what kind of person is a "follower of the Dhamma"?

The person who, practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, possesses a preeminent faculty of wisdom and develops the noble path led by wisdom and preceded by wisdom—this person is called a "follower of the Dhamma.
A person practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry is a follower of the Dhamma; one established in the fruit is one who has attained vision.
And what kind of person is a follower by faith (*saddhānusārī*)?
It is that person who, practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, possesses a preeminent faculty of faith and develops the Noble Path carried by faith and preceded by faith—
this is called a person who is a "follower by faith."
The person practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry is one who follows by faith; established in the fruit, they are one liberated by faith.
And what is the person who is "at most seven times reborn"?

Here, a certain person, through the total destruction of the three fetters, becomes a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as their final goal.
Thus, having wandered and transmigrated seven times among gods and humans, he makes an end of suffering—
this person is called "one for whom seven births at most remain.
And what kind of person is "one who goes from family to family"?

Here, a certain person, through the complete destruction of three fetters, becomes a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and having enlightenment as his final goal.
Having wandered and transmigrated among two or three families, he makes an end of suffering—
this is called a person who "goes from family to family" (kolaṅkolo).
And what is the person who is a "single-seed" (ekabījī)?

Here, a certain person, through the total destruction of three fetters, becomes a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and having enlightenment as his final goal.
Having produced only one more human existence, he makes an end of suffering.
This person is called "one who has a single seed.
And what kind of person is a once-returner?

Here, a certain person, through the total destruction of three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, becomes a once-returner; returning only once more to this world, he makes an end of suffering.
This person is called a "once-returner.
And what kind of person is a non-returner?
Here, a certain person, through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there, no longer subject to returning from that world.
This person is called a "non-returner" (anāgāmī).
And what kind of person is one who attains final nibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyī)?

Here, a certain person, through the complete destruction of the five lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṁyojana), becomes spontaneously reborn (opapātiko) and attains final nibbāna there, being of a nature not to return from that world.
Having been reborn there, either immediately or before reaching the midpoint of the lifespan, one generates the noble path for the sake of abandoning the higher fetters—
this person is called an "antarāparinibbāyī" (one who attains parinirvāṇa in the interval).
And what kind of person is an "upahaccaparinibbāyī" (one who attains parinirvāṇa upon reaching)?
Here, a certain person, through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, is of spontaneous birth (*opapātiko*), attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to returning from that world.
Having passed beyond the middle of his lifespan, or having reached it, he brings forth the Noble Path for the abandoning of the higher fetters—
this person is called one who "attains Nibbāna upon reaching" (*upahaccaparinibbāyī*).
And what kind of person is one who attains final nibbāna without exertion?
Here, a certain person, through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, is of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there, not subject to returning from that world.
He generates the noble path without exertion for the sake of abandoning the higher fetters.
This person is called one who attains final nibbāna without exertion (*asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī*).
And what kind of person is one who attains final nibbāna with exertion (*sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī*)?

Here, a certain person, through the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, becomes of spontaneous birth (*opapātiko*), attaining final nibbāna there, no longer subject to returning from that world.
Thus, by means of volitional effort, he generates the noble path for the abandoning of the higher fetters;
this person is called one who attains final nibbāna with exertion.
And what kind of person is one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm?

Here, a certain person, through the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, becomes one of spontaneous birth (*opapātiko*), attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to returning from that world.

Having passed away from the Aviha realm, he goes to Atappa; having passed away from Atappa, he goes to Sudassa; having passed away from Sudassa, he goes to Sudassī; having passed away from Sudassī, he goes to Akaniṭṭha.
In Akaniṭṭha, he generates the Noble Path for the abandoning of the higher fetters.
This person is called one who "flows upwards, bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm.
And what person is a stream-enterer practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry?
A person practicing for the abandoning of the three fetters is one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry.
The person for whom the three fetters have been abandoned is called a "stream-enterer.
A person who has practiced for the thinning of sensual desire and ill will is one practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning.
The person for whom sensual desire and ill will have been attenuated is called a "once-returner.
A person who is practicing for the complete abandonment of sensual desire and ill will is one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning.
The person for whom sensual desire and ill will have been abandoned without remainder—
this person is called a "non-returner" (anāgāmī).

A person who is practicing for the complete abandonment of attachment to the fine-material realm, attachment to the immaterial realm, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance is one practicing for the realization of the fruit of arahantship.
The person for whom sensual lust for the realm of form, sensual lust for the formless realm, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance have been abandoned without remainder—
this person is called an "Arahant.
This is the exposition of the single [type].
